newsitem.title: CHINA: Political minuet as China mourns Deng.
newsitem.headline: Political minuet as China mourns Deng.

text.p: Shrouded in secrecy, Chinese leaders on Friday began political shadow plays around the body of Deng Xiaoping as they planned his funeral and their own careers without the patriach.

The funeral will be a simple farewell: no overseas dignitaries, no foreign media, no lying in state -- and no tomb. Deng's corneas will be donated to an eye bank, his body offered for dissection and his ashes scattered into the sea according to the wishes of his family.

Political analysts said the size of a 459-strong funeral committee led by Deng's protege Jiang Zemin illuminated arcane succession politics unchanged since the days when emperors ruled from the Dragon Throne of Beijing's Forbidden City.
An all-embracing "who's who" of the Chinese leadership was intended as a show of unity, they said.
It also helped conceal the inner workings of the Communist Party as key figures jockeyed for position before the 15th party congress next October when top posts and policies will be revealed.
A smaller group might have made it easier for outsiders to speculate on who is in and who is out.

In imperial China, the transfer of the "mandate of heaven" to a new emperor was rarely smooth. While the latest power shift so far has been seamless, analysts said later upheavals could not be ruled out.

Jiang, 70, must now confront his own mortality and fend off other aspirants to power, among them Qiao Shi, the former security tsar who now heads parliament, economic supremo Zhu Rongji and premier Li Peng.
China's propaganda machine on Friday went into overdrive, hailing the diminutive Deng as a giant whose stature could never be matched and pledging the army's loyalty to his political heirs.
As flags around the capital flew at half-mast on the second day of official mourning for Deng, who died on Wednesday at 92, the judiciary sounded a cautious note with calls for stability.
Security was discreet and the atmosphere calm in the capital. People hurried to work as usual usual on a bright and crisp Friday morning.
But hundreds of grieving people gathered in Deng's birthplace Paifang, a tiny village in southwestern Sichuan, some falling to their knees in tears.
Police armed with assault rifles rolled up to ensure order, local officials said. No incidents were reported.
"Comrade Deng Xiaoping... became a great son of the people, a giant who will never be matched," the People's Daily said in a commentary. "The people of the motherland love and esteem him."
Asian leaders sounded more glowing tributes to Deng but Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui struck a discordant note by saying the island had weathered worse storms.
"We should not take this issue too seriously," Lee was quoted as telling a group of national assemblymen on the island that China maintains is a rebellious province.
Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew said Deng's spirit and courage never failed and he helped set the stage for China to become a heavyweight nation.
"He saved China. Without him, China could have been like the Soviet Union. Instead China will become a huge heavyweight nation in 30 years," Lee said in a letter to Jiang.
Authorities cancelled most celebrations for China's annual lantern festival in a gesture of respect to Deng's memory.
The festival ending lunar new year celebrations is a time when Chinese string up brightly coloured lamps, traditionally in paper, in parks around the country.
Stocks in China and Taiwan rose on Friday while those in Hong Kong fell as investors shrugged off Deng's death and began to focus once more on economic fundamentals.
The markets had ended higher on Thursday once Deng's death was perceived as removing a major element of uncertainty from the markets.
Brokers said securities houses in Shanghai held meetings on Wednesday and agreed on the need to keep markets stable but not intervene to support them.
